title: Will devolving tax powers to mayors and cities narrow England’s divides?
label: 20 October 2026 · Fiscal devolution in England
summary: Witnesses from Centre for Cities, Core Cities UK and Key Cities discussed whether giving mayors and combined (mayoral strategic) authorities more tax-raising power will boost growth, how to share and equalise funds, which decisions belong at which level, accountability risks, and whether local councils have the skills and staff to make devolution work. They agreed devolution can help but is no silver bullet, needs predictable rules, clear roles, capacity-building and mechanisms to protect struggling places.

glossary.definition: Mayoral strategic authority — a combined area led by an elected mayor, responsible for strategic functions like transport and planning.
A single-tier local council that handles all local services in its area, unlike a two-tier county/district system.
A way to share revenue so poorer or slower-growing places still get enough money for basic services.
Known multi-year central government funding packages for a place, used as a baseline in funding swaps.
A tax on business property that currently funds local services and is often discussed for local retention or reform.
A local plan, agreed with employers, to shape skills and training provision in an area.
A power allowing a mayor or central body to take a local planning decision out of the hands of a local council.

chapters.title: Does fiscal devolution raise growth?
chapters.takeaway: There is some evidence devolution helps growth, but causation is unclear and outcomes will vary by place.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: First: will fiscal devolution boost economic growth, and will it help all places equally?

turns.speaker: Andrew Carter
turns.text: There is some international evidence—wages and productivity are slightly higher where powers are local—but causation is hard to prove. Devolution is one useful intervention, not a miracle cure, and it may be better than the current, highly centralised status quo.

turns.speaker: Stephen Jones
turns.text: The tricky part is the counterfactual: separating what local decisions did from broader economic change. The stronger evidence is about capability—places where local leaders respond quickly and coordinate with businesses and universities tend to get better results.

turns.speaker: Councillor Vince Maple
turns.text: It’s not the fiscal power itself but better local decisions, closer relationships and being able to spot and prevent problems early. Places start from different positions; devolution helps some levers but won’t erase long-term deprivation on its own.

chapters.title: Replacing grants with tax shares: short-term certainty and equalisation
chapters.takeaway: Swapping some grant for income-tax shares can give incentives, but needs predictable equalisation so places aren’t penalised unfairly.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is what ministers propose really devolution, or just reshuffling central grants with a new formula?

turns.speaker: Andrew Carter
turns.text: It’s more than a formula swap. Replacing fixed grants with a share of local tax links funding to local growth, giving places more flexibility and some upside if their tax base expands. But you must manage short-term certainty during transition.

turns.speaker: Councillor Vince Maple
turns.text: Places will worry about parity: many big towns still lack MSAs. Certainty matters; a two- to three-year integrated settlement replaced by an equivalent tax share could give short-term predictability.

turns.speaker: Lord Young of Cookham
turns.text: How can we tell if extra local receipts came from local choices or from national economic growth?

turns.speaker: Andrew Carter
turns.text: You can’t fully disentangle that. The solution is designing mechanisms that reward growth while accepting some noise from the national economy, and testing arrangements over a couple of years.

turns.speaker: Stephen Jones
turns.text: Equalisation needs to be predictable and ongoing. Big resets every five years remove incentives for long-term investment. Models like a small top-slice or a baseline floor keep incentives while protecting places.

turns.speaker: Andrew Carter
turns.text: A Swiss-style benchmark—pooling a share of growth above a threshold and redistributing it—can encourage ambition yet support those lagging behind. It’s feasible and has precedents.

chapters.title: Who should hold what powers: MSAs, councils and communities?
chapters.takeaway: Strategic economic decisions fit MSAs, local services fit councils; one size won’t suit every area and roles must be clear.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should major powers go to MSAs or stay with local authorities?

turns.speaker: Andrew Carter
turns.text: The principle is economic coterminosity: strategic transport, planning and skills work at a wider economic geography, not at small borough level. MSAs make sense there; elsewhere, unitary councils are the right model.

turns.speaker: Stephen Jones
turns.text: We should design four-tier relationships—central, strategic, local and neighbourhood—so each can act where appropriate. The system must build subsidiarity, accountability and joined-up incentives rather than siloed decision-making.

turns.speaker: Councillor Vince Maple
turns.text: Power should sit where it needs to. Many district councils that drive local economies must be heard. Key Cities members outside MSAs want access to powers too; one size doesn’t fit a coastal town and a big urban centre.

turns.speaker: Stephen Jones
turns.text: There’s a real risk of duplication for national businesses or investors if every mayor acts separately. Groups like Core Cities exist to coordinate cities’ voices and avoid that.

chapters.title: Accountability, politics and the mayor’s role
chapters.takeaway: Mayors raise public awareness and can resolve strategic deadlocks, but call-in powers and majority voting raise tensions that need careful safeguards.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does concentrating power in mayors risk imposing partisan decisions on parts of a city that disagree?

turns.speaker: Stephen Jones
turns.text: It depends on the decision. For genuinely strategic issues that affect the whole city-region—say a major transport or retail artery—there’s legitimacy for mayoral involvement. But mayors acting as a habitual override would be counterproductive.

turns.speaker: Andrew Carter
turns.text: Mayors increase public clarity: polling shows people in mayoral areas know who their mayor is far more than they know their council leader. Call-in powers should be last resort, used sparingly to resolve strategic impasses.

turns.speaker: Councillor Vince Maple
turns.text: The main concern locally is powers moving up from councils to mayors, especially on planning. Some leaders fear losing local say; others accept mayors can help attract investment.

turns.speaker: Stephen Jones
turns.text: Legally, combined authority decisions are taken by the authority (mayor plus council leaders) with majority voting and the mayor often holding a casting vote. In practice, effective places work by ongoing collaboration, not constant voting.

turns.speaker: Andrew Carter
turns.text: If voters dislike the outcomes they can change the mayor or councils at election time. But there’s a design challenge: you need some downside to local decisions so incentives remain, while having emergency national backstops for major failure.

chapters.title: Capacity, timing and a pragmatic road map
chapters.takeaway: Devolution needs transfers of staff, steady funding, predictable equalisation and clarity on roles; a phased roadmap and capacity-building matter more than instant universal rollout.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are local councils ready for these changes? Will capacity be sucked into mayoral offices?

turns.speaker: Councillor Vince Maple
turns.text: Local officers are resilient and talented, but the Government’s pause on reorganisation has left staff uncertain. Some will move to new strategic roles, others will stay; the transition must be managed so services don’t suffer.

turns.speaker: Stephen Jones
turns.text: We must do organised workforce and organisational design: identify what skills are needed where, transfer headcount and budgets where appropriate, and avoid simply shifting people from one public job to another without net gain.

turns.speaker: Andrew Carter
turns.text: Think system-wide: central departments should shrink where responsibilities move outwards. National agencies—Homes England, UKRI, etc.—also need to redeploy staff into places. The future test is not how many Whitehall officials remain, but how well places are supported.

turns.speaker: Councillor Vince Maple
turns.text: Practical unfairness already exists: examples like apprenticeship brokerage funding going only to MSAs leave unitary and non-MSA areas feeling they miss out. That undermines trust in the rollout.

turns.speaker: Stephen Jones
turns.text: The Budget is a stepping stone, not the finish. Revenue shares, business-rate reform and motoring taxes are all areas for further, careful design. A roadmap that builds capability, predictable rules and a modest equalisation top-slice will keep incentives for growth.

turns.speaker: Andrew Carter
turns.text: A practical metric: increase the share of locally-raised tax retained locally from roughly 5% today towards 10–15% over time. That would be meaningful but still cautious.

turns.speaker: Councillor Vince Maple
turns.text: Above all, clarify what 'fiscal devolution' actually means for each place, co-produce the design with local government, and fix outdated things like council tax to modernise the tax base.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. The evidence is clear: devolution can help but needs predictable rules, clarity on roles, built capacity and fair equalisation to avoid making some places worse off.
